extracted.intended_audience: educated, politically engaged readers (British public, parliamentarians, and political thinkers)
extracted.subtask_description: An eighteenth-century political essay arguing normative principles about constitution, administration, and dangers of court favoritism; prescribes how appointments, ministerial power, and institutional checks ought to operate in a free state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary powers exercised on public principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The discretionary powers which are necessarily vested in the monarch ... should all be exercised upon public principles and national grounds, and not on the likings or prejudices, the intrigues or policies, of a court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws alone are insufficient; the exercise of nomination, revenue, conduct of peace and war, and execution must be guided by public/national grounds. If discretionary powers are used for private favoritism, the spirit and effectiveness of the constitution are subverted. Ministers' prudence and uprightness are central to keeping the commonwealth a living constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration correspondent to the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Every sort of government ought to have its administration correspondent to its legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The composition of the executive should match the character and source of the legislature: in free states, the executory system must be dependent on, and acceptable to, parliamentary and popular principles. Mismatch causes disorder and weakens the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular control over magistrates, rewards, and honors
rubrics_metrics.description: The popular election of magistrates, and popular disposition of rewards and honors, is one of the first advantages of a free state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where direct popular election is not feasible, the constitution should secure the effects of popular choice (through Parliament and representatives). This popular control is necessary to preserve freedom and the energizing effects of good government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary refusal as a constitutional control
rubrics_metrics.description: It had always been held the first duty of Parliament to refuse to support government, until power was in the hands of persons who were acceptable to the people, or while factions predominated in the court in which the nation had no confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliament must retain the negative power of withholding support to hold ministers accountable; passive acquiescence will enable bad men to entrench and fortify themselves under pretence of fair trial, ultimately subverting constitutional balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions must prevent malfeasance as well as remedy it
rubrics_metrics.description: Every good political institution must have a preventive operation as well as a remedial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutions to exclude unfit or corrupt persons from power proactively rather than relying solely on punishment afterward, since punishment is often tardy and uncertain and may fall on the injured rather than the criminal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due arrangement of trustworthy men in active offices
rubrics_metrics.description: The due arrangement of men in the active part of the state ... ought to be among its very first and dearest objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing competent, reputable individuals in active posts is essential for effective government; attention to personnel is not secondary but foundational. Neglecting appointments allows parts of government to languish or be perverted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior proven conduct as a qualification for high trusts
rubrics_metrics.description: Before men are put forward into the great trusts of the state, they ought by their conduct to have obtained such a degree of estimation in their country, as may be some sort of pledge and security to the public, that they will not abuse those trusts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection for office should be based on demonstrated public conduct and reputation that pledges future trustworthiness — not on court favor, intrigue, or ephemeral proximity to power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of systemic favoritism and personal patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: A plan of favoritism for our executory government is essentially at variance with the plan of our legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems that insert favoritism—placing insulated creatures in households and secondary offices with life-like tenure, occupying avenues to the throne—undermine representative government, create unaccountable power centres, and weaken national strength. Executive arrangements should resist such patronage networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers must actively sustain the laws and functions of state
rubrics_metrics.description: Without them [ministers], your commonwealth is no better than a scheme upon paper; ministers may suffer one part of government to languish, another to be perverted from its purposes ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ministers have active responsibility to execute laws, maintain institutional functions, and prevent decay; negligence, ignorance, or bad design by ministers can render laws ineffective even where legal rules exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration should not be deliberately weakened to aggrandize the court
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan proceeds expressly on the idea of enfeebling the regular executory power. It proceeds on the idea of weakening the state in order to strengthen the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schemes that deliberately weaken ministry or executive capacity to increase court influence are condemned; a healthy constitution requires substantive strength in administration, not a façade of royal splendor built on a debilitated government.
